column5: seedtime and harvest continue as long as the earth remains
column6: The commentary makes crop growth culminate in what remains; Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest will not cease while the earth remains, giving the agricultural cycle an explicit duration.

column5: Ruth asks to glean ears of grain in a field
column6: The commentary treats a share from the crop as a right given; Ruth's request and gleaning in Boaz's field narrate a vulnerable foreign widow receiving harvest produce under Israel's field practice.

column5: workers pull grain from bundles and leave it for Ruth to glean
column6: The commentary's field yields an owed portion; Boaz orders extra grain deliberately left for Ruth, showing a landowner expanding the harvest share through generous care.

column5: the king takes a tenth of seed and vineyard produce
column6: The commentary defines kharāj as a known amount removed from property each year; Samuel warns that a king will take a tenth of grain and vineyard yield, a political levy that makes the fixed crop share a contested claim.

column5: openhanded aid to the poor is followed by blessing on all work
column6: The commentary connects giving a crop share with cleansing and remaining good; Deuteronomy commands giving to the poor and promises blessing on the giver's work, joining generosity to productive success.

column5: honor YHWH with wealth and first fruits of all produce
column6: The commentary's harvest has a portion due; Proverbs makes first fruits the way to honor YHWH, identifying agricultural priority as a form of payment and devotion.

column5: full barns and overflowing wine vats follow first fruits
column6: The commentary says the given share purifies the remainder; Proverbs places full barns and vats after first-fruit honor, giving a direct promise of abundance alongside the due.

column5: seed of peace, fruitful vine, productive ground, and dew
column6: The commentary joins field growth to good that lasts; Zechariah brings seed, vine, land produce, and dew together as a restored blessing, combining crop fertility with peace.

column5: tree by water stays green in heat and never ceases bearing fruit
column6: The commentary contrasts pasture that dries with productive growth that remains; Jeremiah's water-rooted tree does not fear drought and keeps yielding fruit, making endurance explicit.

column5: earth yields increase and God blesses
column6: The commentary attributes growth to divine blessing; the psalm says the earth has yielded its increase and God blesses, directly joining harvest and blessing.

column5: distributes freely to the poor; righteousness endures forever
column6: The commentary links the crop's given share to lasting good; the psalm joins generous distribution to the poor with righteousness that endures, a close ethical counterpart to a purifying share and permanent success.

column5: first-ripe barley loaves are brought to Elisha
column6: The commentary's yield has a portion paid out; a man brings first-fruit barley bread to the prophet, narrating produce set aside as a sacred share.

column5: a small barley offering feeds a hundred with some left over
column6: The commentary follows a crop's given share with what remains; Elisha distributes the offering, a hundred eat, and food remains, adding miraculous increase and remainder to the harvest image.

column5: one-sixth ephah from each homer of wheat and barley
column6: The commentary defines the annual kharāj as a known amount removed from property; Ezekiel specifies a measured grain contribution, an exact agricultural counterpart to a fixed due.

column5: oil contribution measured against the homer
column6: The commentary's crop share is measured and paid; Ezekiel likewise sets an oil contribution by a defined volume, extending measured dues from grain to another product.

column5: do not plow injustice or sow its furrows, lest you reap it manyfold
column6: The commentary makes plowing and growth a figure for success; Sirach turns furrowing and reaping into moral consequence, adding a warning that unjust cultivation multiplies its own return.

column5: charity as the salt that preserves wealth
column6: The commentary says a paid share purifies what remains; the rabbinic saying calls charity the salt of wealth, interpreting giving as what preserves a person's remaining property.

column5: bear fruit worthy of repentance
column6: The commentary joins purification to a productive crop; John demands fruit that fits repentance, making agricultural yield an observable ethical consequence of cleansing.

column5: share a second tunic and food with someone who has none
column6: The commentary says a portion from one's produce is given; John's answer turns repentance into sharing clothing and food, making the purifying act materially concrete.

column5: tax collectors must collect no more than the assigned amount
column6: The commentary defines kharāj as a known amount taken from property; John tells tax collectors not to collect beyond what is ordered, making fixed dues an ethical boundary against extraction.

column5: tithing herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faith
column6: The commentary links paying a crop's share to purification; Jesus says exact tithing must not displace justice, mercy, and faith, qualifying the claim that payment alone cleans the remainder.

column5: first blade, then ear, then full grain on the stalk
column6: The commentary unfolds soil-breaking into seed growth and lasting yield; Mark specifies the intermediate stages of that growth before the ripe harvest, preserving the crop's full sequence.

column5: the plowman plows in hope and the thresher hopes to share the crop
column6: The commentary names the farmer through breaking soil and gives the crop a due share; Paul says agricultural workers labor in hope of sharing the produce, directly joining cultivation and right to yield.

column5: gift to Paul becomes fruit increasing to the giver's account
column6: The commentary links the crop's paid share to lasting good; Paul calls the Philippians' material gift fruit accruing to their account, recasting generosity as a yield that lasts.

column5: all flesh is grass and its glory like a flower that fades
column6: The commentary contrasts perishing pasture with lasting good; Peter applies Isaiah's grass-and-flower image to human life, making the pasture's decay a figure for mortal transience.

column5: the Lord's word remains forever and is the preached gospel
column6: The commentary sets fading growth against what endures; Peter continues the grass quotation by identifying the enduring word with the gospel preached to the audience, giving Isaiah's plant contrast a Christian proclamation context.

column5: earth sprouts and garden makes seed grow; righteousness and praise spring up
column6: The commentary joins crop growth to purification and success; Isaiah compares the earth's sprouting to righteousness and praise springing before nations, bringing agricultural and ethical growth together.

column5: field grass is alive today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, yet clothed by God
column6: The commentary uses withering pasture as the transient outcome; Jesus also makes field grass short-lived, but uses God's care for it to argue trust, giving ephemeral growth a positive theological value.

column5: God gives each seed its own body
column6: The commentary attributes seed growth to divine blessing; Paul says God gives the seed its body as God wills, making the source of differentiated growth explicitly divine.

column5: tree of life bears monthly fruit and its leaves heal nations
column6: The commentary links growth with what remains good; Revelation's final-city tree yields continually and heals the nations, giving enduring fruit an afterlife setting.
